subject: Scaling & latency validation playbook for AtlasHealth RFP
messages:

Subject: RFP appendix: performance & validation expectations

Soojin,

Thanks again for the overview last week. The procurement team asked us to provide a concise performance appendix for the RFP that covers the following for your platform:
- single-request P99 latency (for 8k and 32k contexts)
- sustained throughput (tokens/sec) at 95% utilization for a 10k concurrent session workload
- test methodology including workload shaping, token distribution, and warm-up behavior
- failover behavior under simulated GPU loss and autoscaling timelines

Attached is the RFP appendix (AtlasHealth_RFP_Performance_Appendix.pdf). Can Redwood provide a reproducible test plan and an initial set of results or expected profiles we can include in our submission? If you have a short playbook we typically include that too.

Timeline: we need an initial write-up by EOD 2026-05-06, and a reproducible config (YAML or k8s job) that our infra team can run by 2026-05-13.

Let me know if you need any additional inputs (sample prompt sets, tokenization details, or a dedicated test account).

Best,
John

Subject: Re: RFP appendix: performance & validation expectations

John / Priya,

Appreciate the clear ask and the timeline — we can definitely provide a reproducible test plan and an initial performance profile for AtlasHealth. I attached a short playbook and a sample test-config you can run in your environment. High-level approach below; full details are in redwood-probe-playbook-v1.pdf.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Objectives: measure P50/P95/P99 latency for representative prompt mixes at 8k and 32k context; measure sustained tokens/sec and concurrency behavior; validate graceful degradation and autoscale recovery.
- Test harness: k6 for request shaping + a lightweight runner that drives the Redwood inference endpoint (auth token + model variant). We provide a Kubernetes job YAML (test-config-sample.yml) and a small container (image reference in the playbook).
- Key steps:
  1) Baseline warm-up (30–60 min) with low QPS to populate KV cache and warm CUDA kernels.
  2) Incremental ramp (10% increments every 3 minutes) up to target concurrency to map the knee of the curve.
  3) Sustained soak (60 minutes) at target throughput to record steady-state metrics and error budgets.
  4) Failure injection: simulate a worker loss and observe failover (route + autoscale) and cold-start tail-latency for in-flight sessions.
- Metrics we collect: per-request latency histogram (p50/95/99), tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization, memory/KV cache hit rate, queue lengths, and error codes.

Open questions for AtlasHealth (to make the configs deterministic):
- Which model family and tokenizer do you plan to use (open model name + quantization)? Tokenization affects token counts and throughput.
- Typical prompt length distribution (avg prompt tokens, avg generated tokens) and expected top_k/top_p settings.
- Network egress constraints (if you plan to run tests from a constrained subnet).

Deliverables and dates:
- EOD 2026-05-06: Short playbook + expected numbers and sample configs (we'll deliver this).
- 2026-05-10: We can run a hosted Redwood verification run (on Redwood Dedicated) and share raw metrics/graphs if you grant a temporary test account.
- 2026-05-13: Reproducible YAML/runner you can execute in Atlas infra.

I've looped in Ben and Marissa to confirm resource availability for the hosted verification run and to coordinate an eng contact for failure-injection scenarios.

Attachment: redwood-probe-playbook-v1.pdf; please review and flag anything you want added.

Thanks,
Soojin Lee

Soojin —
Quick confirm on capacity and ops for the hosted verification run:

- Rishi will own failure-injection (we'll spin a canary pool and kill one node during soak).
- Ops note: please advise Atlas to keep the prompt set deterministic and provide a seed file — nondeterministic generation (live user traffic) makes reproducibility difficult.

Marissa — can you provide the sample Grafana dashboard and the Prometheus scrape config we should share with Atlas (to collect GPU metrics and queue-level stats)?
